title: The Foreign Controller reuses the mainnet controller's procedures verbatim, so Grove's safety properties are chain-invariant
content:
A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.2.2.1.2.3 opens the `ForeignController` specification, and almost every child is a pointer rather than a procedure: setting mint recipients, LayerZero recipients, max slippage, tick bounds, TWAP seconds and max exchange rate (A...3.1.1–A...3.1.10), removing a relayer (A...3.2.1), and the CCTP, LayerZero, ERC-20, ERC-4626, ERC-7540, Centrifuge, Aave, Curve, Merkl and Pendle operations (A...3.3.2–A...3.3.11) are each declared to be "the same as through the Monolithic Mainnet Controller contract."

Specifying by reference rather than by restatement is a claim about the system, not just an editorial economy. It means the role separation, the slippage floors, the fail-closed configuration checks and the rate-limit semantics documented for mainnet hold identically on every foreign deployment. An auditor or relayer who has learned one controller has learned them all, and a change to a shared procedure cannot drift between chains.

What differs is the **set** of available integrations, and the differences are informative. The `ForeignController` adds first-class PSM deposit and withdraw functions (A...3.3.1.1, A...3.3.1.2). It has no Ethena, no sUSDe cooldown and no DAI-USDS migrator, because USDe minting and the DAI-USDS parity contract exist only on Ethereum. A...3.1.9 also adds a mainnet-absent admin function, `setMerklDistributor`, since the distributor address is chain-specific.

The underlying principle: keep the security model uniform across deployments and let the deployment vary only in which external protocols it can reach.
description: Nearly every ForeignController admin, freezer and relayer function is specified only as a cross-reference to its mainnet counterpart; chains differ in which integrations exist, not in how they behave.
